newsitem.title: ITALY: Piaggio chief sees upturn in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Piaggio chief sees upturn in 1997.

text.p: Italian motor scooter maker Piaggio Veicoli Europei SpA, celebrating the 50th anniversary of its most famous product, the Vespa, said market conditions were tough this year but it expected an upturn in 1997.

Piaggio chairman Giovanni Alberto Agnelli told Reuters in an interview at the weekend that the group's top priority was to boost its presence in south-east Asia and would consider a flotation "when the market conditions are favourable".
"Turnover is a little bit higher this year -- around four to five percent," Agnelli said. But he added:
"Profits should be much lower...We're a big exporter so the revaluation of the lira has hurt us a lot. I think 1997 will be a better year than 1996."
Piaggio made a net profit of 15 billion lire ($9.84 million) in 1995 on turnover of 2.1 trillion lire.

Agnelli said the Vespa, the humble little scooter that was named after a wasp and launched a cheap new means of transport in post-war Italy when it rolled off the production line in 1946, was still one of the company's best-selling products.
He was speaking after the launch of two new models of the cult classic that came to epitomise Rome's "dolce vita", featuring environmentally-friendly engines and sleeker styling.
"We've already had 15,000 orders," Agnelli said. "Our forecast for next year is around 50,000-60,000 vehicles. I think this certainly should be met."
But Agnelli ruled out a stock market listing immediately.

"Italian financial markets are under serious investigation from the international financial community and with the privatisation plans already announced, I don't think it's a serious possibility in the next eight, 10, 15 months," he said.
"But yes...when the market conditions are favourable, we will consider a flotation," he added.

Italy's bourse has been in the spotlight in recent weeks as a crisis at information technology group Olivetti has prompted a rash of resignations at the top of the company and a plunge in its share prices.
The government is planning the privatisations of telephone group Stet and electricity giant Enel in 1997.

Agnelli, the 32-year-old nephew and annointed heir of former Fiat cars chairman Gianni Agnelli, took the helm of Piaggio in 1993 and has been driving it into Asian markets where growth has been dynamic and "there is certainly room to expand".
"In India, we're growing 20 percent this year...We have around 10-15 percent with our partner LML.
"In south east Asia we've had tremendous growth -- we've forecast our growth rate to be 45 percent this year -- because our presence was very limited," he said.
Piaggio leads the European scooter sector and is fourth worldwide behind Japanese giants Honda, Suzuki and Yamaha,
Agnelli estimated Piaggio now had two to three percent of the southeast Asian market but said he was "not even considering ever reaching the European market share" of 40-45 percent.
He said southern Europe was in recession and "the market has been practically blocked" but Germany was strong and volumes were growing at around 40 percent in England against last year.
The new Vespa will now meet emission regulations in North America but Agnelli said that market was not a priority.
"We are attentively studying the North American market...but I think at the moment our priorities are more focused in Asia."
However Agnelli said China had proved a tougher market to crack than expected and Piaggio had "slowed down" plans there. ($1=1524 Lire)
